goals.question: Summarise in a few sentences what the main theorem says about multiplying two n-bit integers, in which machine model it holds, which earlier conjecture it refutes, and the overall plan the proof follows to get there.

key_points.point: One deterministic machine with a fixed alphabet and a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes multiplies two n-bit numbers exactly in time O(n (log n)^(1-kappa)), with kappa = 2^-182 > 0.
This is asymptotically faster than n log n, so it refutes the 1971 Schoenhage-Strassen guess that n log n is optimal for multitape machines.

The plan is to build two cheaper tape primitives (swapping address chunks and a combined butterfly layer), use them to speed up Fourier-style transforms and ring convolution, and reduce the integer product to such convolutions.
The result is exact because the accumulated numerical error on the recovered coefficients is below 1/2, so rounding gives the true integers; the cost total then shows a power of log n is saved.

goals.question: Why can the log n factor in n log n only be beaten here by making address movement and butterfly arithmetic cheaper, rather than by some other tweak of a standard FFT-style multiplier? What accounting of a standard transform on a tape machine leads to this?

key_points.point: A transform on Theta(n) stored bits has about log n levels, and a tape machine must scan the whole array to do each level.
Each full scan costs time linear in the data, so scanning per level adds up to n log n for the whole transform.

So to get below n log n, many levels must be handled in one pass: moving data between address positions and doing butterfly arithmetic on several address bits together must cost less than one pass each.
This is why the proof builds the chunk-interchange and simultaneous-layer primitives with sub-linear cost per unit of data per level.

goals.question: The two tape primitives get a saving that is tiny yet strictly positive (an exponent just below 1). Explain why the recursive construction produces a genuine power saving, and why the whole thing hinges on one strict inequality between the number of smaller calls s and W times m.

key_points.point: A call at parameter m times f is implemented by s calls at parameter f, each on a stream holding only 1/W of the data volume.
So per unit of data, going up by a factor m in the parameter multiplies the recursive cost by s/W, whereas a linear-cost operation would multiply it by m.
If s < W*m then s/W < m, so the recursion solves to a power of the parameter strictly below the first power; if s were equal to W*m there would be no saving.

The strict inequality comes from the network labels: the total dimension is fixed by telescoping and only a small number L of unavoidable decreases occur, with L/N < 1/2, leaving s a little under W*m.
Hence the exponent is only barely below 1 (about 1 - 2^-50), but it is still a power saving.

goals.question: Explain how the algorithm turns a product of two integers into transforms of power-of-two length, in order: what each stage in the chain (radix digits, address map, resampling with chirps, twist to the polynomial ring, synthetic-transform convolution) accomplishes and why it is needed for the next stage.

key_points.point: Cutting each integer into radix-2^b digits makes the product a convolution of short integer coefficients, and the padded length S exceeds the product's degree so cyclic wraparound does nothing.
The Chinese-remainder address map re-lays a cyclic convolution of length S as a convolution over several axes of pairwise coprime prime lengths, via cheap triangular controlled shifts.

Prime-length transforms are not directly available from the fast power-of-two machinery, so Gaussian resampling approximates them through nearby power-of-two lengths and the chirp identity converts the remaining permuted transform into a cyclic convolution.
A phase twist converts the last cyclic axis into the ring modulo y^r + 1, where roots of unity are powers of y, so the synthetic transform needs only signed shifts and can use the fast primitives.
After the pointwise product and the opposite transform, rescaling and rounding recover the integer coefficients and carry propagation yields the binary product.

goals.question: Why does kappa equal 2^-182 and not some larger constant? Which part of the cost accounting fixes it, and why is the margin taken to be twice kappa?

key_points.point: After dividing each cost by the volume V = Tp (which is of order n), seven operations dominate, each costing a power of p below 1 with some margin g_i.
The smallest margin is 2^-181, coming from the chunk-exchange row, where it is the product of three tiny fixed exponents: epsilon, c and 1 - tau (2^-75 * 2^-56 * 2^-50).
Leftover powers of log p must be absorbed, and any fixed power of log p is eventually below p raised to a small positive exponent, so a margin of 2*kappa leaves room for that.
Taking the margin 2^-181 as twice kappa gives kappa = 2^-182 and total time O(n (log n)^(1-kappa)); setup and prime search cost o(V) and do not affect it.

goals.question: Gaussian resampling is used so that Fourier transforms of prime length can be done with power-of-two transforms. Why does the algorithm leave the coordinate permutations inside the transform identities instead of executing them, and why do the source permutation and the target permutation both disappear without any sorting?

key_points.point: Executing the permutations would mean sorting data on a tape, costing about t p log t per line, which would cancel the power saving.
The target permutation is absorbed by the chirp identity, because the chirp convolution already reads the permuted frequencies.

The source permutation is attached to both forward transforms and the opposite transform; dilating by a unit modulo s just permutes frequencies in the Fourier sum, so the opposite transform undoes it.

Pointwise products commute with applying the same permutation to both operands, so the product can be formed in permuted order and the permutation cancels, giving the plain convolution divided by S squared.

goals.question: The classical FFT-style approach to multiplying n-bit integers does Theta(log n) levels of butterfly work over Theta(n) stored bits. Why does that alone suggest n log n on a tape machine, and where does the new algorithm look for savings to get below it?

key_points.point: On a tape machine every level of the transform must sweep through all the Theta(n) stored bits, so Theta(log n) levels cost Theta(n log n) in total.

So the log factor can only be beaten by making each level cost less than a full pass: cheaper movement of data between addresses on the tapes, and cheaper butterfly arithmetic that handles several address bits together.
The algorithm builds two such faster tape procedures (exchanging address chunks, and a combined butterfly layer over many axes) and plugs them into the transforms.
The machine has a fixed alphabet, a fixed number of tapes and heads that move one cell per step, so data cannot be reached at random and cost counts moves.

goals.question: Why does a recursive scheme where one call on parameter m*f makes s calls on parameter f, each working on 1/W of the data, give a cost per unit of data that is a power of the parameter strictly below the first power? What exactly must hold for the saving, and how large is it?

key_points.point: Each call splits the data over W streams, so each of its s sub-calls handles only 1/W of the volume. Per unit of data, going from f to m*f therefore multiplies the cost by s/W.
A saving needs s/W to be strictly smaller than m, the factor by which the parameter grew, i.e. s < W*m. If s/W were m, cost would just be linear in the parameter and nothing would be gained.
Solving the recurrence gives cost per unit of data about (s/W)^k for parameter m^k, which is below the parameter raised to a fixed exponent smaller than 1.
The saving is tiny: s/W is only a relative 10^-11 or so below m, so the exponent is just under 1 (1 - 2^-50), but it is positive, and the whole power saving rests on that strict inequality.

goals.question: Summarise in a few sentences how the algorithm turns two n-bit integers into their exact product, naming the main stages in order and saying why the final answer is exact rather than approximate.

key_points.point: The inputs are cut into digits of about log n bits, so the product becomes a cyclic convolution of short integer coefficients. The length is chosen so that nothing wraps around.

A Chinese-remainder re-addressing places this length-S convolution on several axes of pairwise coprime prime lengths, and Gaussian resampling plus chirp identities express the prime-length Fourier transforms through power-of-two transforms, with the awkward coordinate permutations kept inside the identities and never executed.

The convolution is carried out by two forward transforms, a pointwise product and an opposite transform, using synthetic polynomial transforms over y^r+1 whose twiddle factors are cheap signed shifts. A phase twist converts the last cyclic axis to that ring.

After rescaling, the accumulated rounding error on each coefficient is below 1/2 because the working precision has spare bits. Rounding therefore gives the exact integer coefficients, and carry propagation produces the exact 2n-bit product.

runs.answer: The chain turns two n-bit integers into their exact 2n-bit product in five stages, each feeding the next. (1) Radix digits (page vub): each input is written in radix 2^b with b = ceil(log2 n) and q digits, so the product becomes a convolution of short coefficient sequences, and the page shows that the convolution length S is large enough that nothing wraps around, and every coefficient is below 2^{3b}. (2) Address map (page guf): the map Phi sends a convolution of length S = s_1...s_d, with pairwise coprime axis lengths s_i, to a convolution on d axes by moving the data only with controlled shifts and axis reorderings. The page says this 'prepares' the next stage but does not say why the axes must be split, so I take it that the next stage works on each prime axis separately. (3) Resampling with chirps (pages roz, pap, dib): each prime-length transform is re-expressed through a power-of-two length t, with the source and target permutations left in place, so that only power-of-two transforms need a fast algorithm. For even t_i the chirp identity on page pap removes the target permutation: the transform becomes a chirp phase, a convolution of length T, and another chirp phase, so the permutation is absorbed into the convolution and never executed as a sort. (4) Twist to the polynomial ring (page taf): multiplying coefficient k of the last cyclic axis of length r by zeta^k, with zeta = e^{pi i/r}, turns that axis into the coordinate of the ring with y^r = -1; a wrap-around then carries a sign that exactly cancels the twist, so convolution along that axis becomes ring convolution, and the twist is undone afterwards. (5) Synthetic-transform convolution (pages tab and kur): the ring convolution over the remaining axes is computed from two forward transforms, M pointwise ring products, and the opposite transform, then scaled by M. Back on page siz, the scalings by S undo the 1/S normalizations, the result is multiplied by 2^{2b+4} S, rounded to the nearest integers, mapped back by Phi inverse, and carries are propagated to give the 2n-bit product, with total error below 1/2 so rounding is exact. The step from stage 3 to 4 and the claim that the twist is what makes the synthetic transform applicable are the weakest links; I followed the algebra but could not verify the cited error bounds.

runs.answer: Split each n-bit input into q = ceiling(n/b) digits in radix 2^b, where b = ceiling(log2 n). Their product is the wrap-around product (the wiki's Cyclic convolution) of the two digit sequences, padded to a length S that is a product of distinct odd primes with T/2 < S < T, and no wrap-around occurs because the padded length is large enough. The sequence is then reindexed onto prime-length axes by a fixed reindexing map (the Chinese-remainder address map page). Each prime-length transform (the wiki's Discrete Fourier transform) is computed through a power-of-two transform, using a resampling identity with fixed linear contractions and phase multipliers (Gaussian resampling and Bluestein chirp identity), with the permutations kept inside the identity so none is executed as a sort. The stages in order are: radix digits; reindexing onto prime axes; two forward transforms of the two sequences; pointwise product of the transforms; one opposite transform; rescaling by S and by 2^(2b+4)S; rounding each entry to the nearest integer; undoing the reindexing; and carry propagation in radix 2^b, which outputs exactly 2n bits. The result is exact rather than approximate because all values are kept to p = 6b fractional bits and the accumulated error on each coefficient is below 1/2; the true coefficients are integers, so rounding returns them exactly, and carry propagation then gives the exact binary product. I am not fully sure of the constants: the wiki's exactness bound is stated only for digit widths b at least 2^24, and I did not see why the prime-length detour is needed.

runs.answer: The chain runs in six stages, each one reducing the product to something the next stage can handle. (1) Radix digits (page vub): each n-bit integer is written as q = ceil(n/b) digits in radix 2^b, with b = ceil(log2 n). The digit product is a wrap-around product (the wiki's Cyclic convolution) of length S, and S is long enough that nothing wraps and every coefficient fits in 3b bits, so the integer product becomes a Cyclic convolution of short coefficients. (2) Address map (page guf): S is a product of pairwise coprime lengths s_1..s_d. The map sending x to the product of x_i raised to mu_i is an isomorphism that preserves Cyclic convolution, so the single length-S Cyclic convolution becomes a d-axis one, with one axis per s_i. This is needed because the later stages act on one axis at a time. (3) Resampling and chirps (pages roz and pap): a transform of prime length s is re-expressed through a transform of a nearby power-of-two length t, so only power-of-two transforms need a fast algorithm. For even t_i the chirp identity gives Q F_t u = conj(a) times (a Cyclic convolution (conj(a) times u)) divided by T, so the target reordering is absorbed into an ordinary Cyclic convolution of power-of-two length T, between two pointwise phase multiplications. (4) Twist (page taf, with page reb): the last cyclic axis is turned into the ring R_r = C[y]/(y^r+1) by multiplying entry k by zeta^k with zeta = e^(pi i/r). The wrap sign of ring multiplication then reproduces the Cyclic convolution on that axis. This is needed because in R_r multiplying by a power of y is only a signed shift, so the transforms over the ring need no complex multiplications. (5) Synthetic-transform convolution (pages tab and gip): both operands are transformed over R_r with roots of unity omega_t = y^(2r/t), multiplied record by record in the ring, and transformed back, with a scaling by the number of records. (6) Assembly and rounding (page siz): after the two forward transforms, the pointwise product, the opposite transform, a rescaling by S, and multiplication by 2^(2b+4) S, the values are rounded to integers, mapped back by the inverse address map, and carries are propagated to give the exact 2n-bit product. Rounding is exact because the error is below 1/2, a claim the page cites to another page that I did not open. Confidence is moderate: I could follow the stage-by-stage reductions and their size bookkeeping, but I took the error bounds and the cited lemmas on trust.

runs.answer: The saving comes from a per-level recurrence. A call at parameter mf splits its data into W streams of volume V/W and makes s smaller calls on them, where s is the total rank of the edge changes and each unit of rank is one smaller call. Writing C(f) for the time per unit volume at parameter f, the children cost s(V/W)C(f), so C(mf) <= (s/W)C(f) + O(1) with C(1) = O(1) (Recursive power saving). Unrolling over the log_m f levels gives C(f) = O(sum_j (s/W)^j). If s/W < m^tau with a fixed tau < 1, the sum is O(f^tau), so an interchange costs O(V f^tau) (Recursive power saving). For the bit network tau = 1 - 2^-50. The strict inequality s < Wm is what makes a tau < 1 available: the per-level factor s/W must be below the factor m by which the parameter shrinks. Nested subspace labels and rank deficit gives s_b = Wm - (N - 2L_b) with L_b/N = 100/539 < 1/2, so the deficit N - 2L_b is positive (Nested subspace labels and rank deficit). Recursive power saving turns that deficit into a margin: s/W = m(1 - eta) with eta = 339/(22587335 m), about 1.5e-11, and the exponential estimate m^(1-2^-50) > m(1 - 20*2^-50) > m(1 - eta) = s/W holds because ln m < 20 and eta exceeds 20*2^-50 (Recursive power saving). So the one strict inequality gives an exponent strictly below 1 by a small positive amount. runs.answer: Each n-bit input is cut into q = ceil(n/b) radix-2^b digits, with b = ceil(log2 n), so the product is the wrapped product (the wiki's Cyclic convolution) of the two digit sequences. With a cyclic length S that is a product of distinct odd primes and satisfies T/2 < S < T, nothing wraps and every coefficient is below 2^{3b}. Stage 1: the index map Phi (page Chinese-remainder address map) moves this cyclic product onto a multi-axis array with prime axis lengths s_i. Stage 2: the two source transforms (the wiki's Discrete Fourier transforms) are computed through power-of-two transforms, using a resampling identity (Gaussian resampling) and chirp phases (Bluestein chirp identity), with the coordinate permutations left implicit so that none is executed. Stage 3: the two transforms are multiplied pointwise and truncated to p = 6b fractional bits, the opposite transform is applied, and the result is scaled by 2^{2b+4} S, rounded to the nearest integer, mapped back by Phi inverse, and carry-propagated in radix 2^b to give the exact 2n-bit product. Why it is exact: the page bounds the total error on each scaled coefficient by 448b 2^{gamma-b}, which is below 1/2 once gamma <= b/4; since the true coefficients are integers, rounding to the nearest integer recovers each one exactly. Confidence is moderate: I followed the stage order and checked the no-wraparound inequality, the coefficient bound, the two-point transform example, the chirp identity, and the final scaling arithmetic, but I took the component error bounds and the gamma <= b/4 step on the wiki's word.

This is the same shape as the master theorem for T(n) = a*T(n/b) with a = s and b = m, with an extra factor 1/W per level.
